newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO defence cuts risky, British minister says.
newsitem.headline: NATO defence cuts risky, British minister says.

text.p: British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo warned his NATO allies on Tuesday a freefall in defence spending risked undermining the western defence alliance's capability to act.
Portillo made his comments as a NATO defence review showed the transatlantic alliance's operations in Bosnia had revealed intelligence shortfalls due to lack of money.
NATO officials quoted Portillo as saying that European defence budgets had dropped to 1.9 percent of gross national product and only 14 percent of that went on purchases for modernisation.
That compared with 3.6 percent of Gross National Product (GNP) in the United States, where 26 percent of the funds went on procurement.

The officials said Portillo -- backed by U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry -- said that Europe could only forge a common defence identity as long as it had a defence capability. Portillo asked for a future meeting to discuss funding issues.

NATO officials said that according to the review NATO was able to mount conventional and nuclear attacks in response to outside threats, but that unless the freefall was stopped in its tracks problems would arise in the future.
"There are some glaring shortfalls creeping into the system due to lack of funding," a NATO source said.
"The shortfalls are not showstoppers. Obviously if more money does not become available these would become issues in the future," the source said.
The review urged those on the spending average to stay there and those underneath it to boost spending.
"That's considered by the military authorities as the minimum for sustaining military capability," one source said.
Shortfalls were also identified in the areas of tactical missile defence systems, air defence in the southern region and mobility for rapid reaction forces.

NATO defence ministers meeting earlier in the Nuclear Planning Group -- a hangover from NATO's Cold War posture -- stressed that member states should step up efforts to ensure against risks from nuclear, chemical and biological weapons.
